home.home.hi-i-am-tanmay-currently-a.text: Hi! I am Tanmay, currently a PhD student in the School of Earth and Space Exploration at Arizona State University, advised by Prof. Sanchayeeta Borthakur. My research interests lie broadly in galaxy formation and processes that impact their evolution, primarily using cosmological simulations.

home.about.prior-to-coming-to-asu-i.text: Prior to coming to ASU, I completed my B.Tech in Engineering Physics from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi in July 2023. I also worked as a visiting student at the Raman Research Institute in Bangalore from May to July 2022. I was born and brought up in Lucknow, India.

home.about.my-current-research-uses-cosm.text: My current research uses cosmological simulations and synthetic quasar absorption spectra to study gas associated with galaxies and galaxy groups. I also work on probabilistic spectral classification of AGN and supernovae using Bayesian logic. You can read more about the current projects in the research section, and about non-academic interests under Personal Interests.

home.research.the-intergalactic-and-circ.text: The intergalactic and circumgalactic media shape how galaxies form and evolve. I want to understand how the Mg II absorbers seen in the spectra of background quasars are connected to galaxies.

home.research.using-mock-quasar-absorpti.text: Using mock quasar absorption spectra generated from cosmological simulations such as IllustrisTNG and SIMBA, I am asking whether these absorbers come from material blown out by star-forming galaxies or from large rotating disks accreting gas onto them.

home.research.o-vi-in-the-intra-group.text: O VI in the Intra-group Medium

home.research.i-compare-o-vi-absorption-.text: I compare O VI absorption in synthetic quasar spectra of 14 galaxy groups each from TNG50 and SIMBA, with 90,000 sightlines per group, against the COS-IGrM survey. Both simulations fall short of the observed covering fraction: 20.6 ± 2.6% in TNG50 and 6.0 ± 0.8% in SIMBA, against 44 ± 5% in COS-IGrM. About 95% of the simulated absorbers are gravitationally bound, and in TNG50 the strongest sit within about 200 kpc of star-forming galaxies, which SIMBA does not show. I published this as a first-author paper in The Astrophysical Journal.

home.research.spectral-classification-of.text: Spectral Classification of AGN and Supernovae

home.research.i-am-building-a-contingent.text: I am building a contingent Bayesian-logic (BLOG) model that classifies AGN and supernova spectra from emission-line detections, widths and ratios. The model includes dust attenuation and variability, and a line-fitting and identification pipeline I built informs its priors. Along the way I wrote a BLOG language extension for VS Code, with syntax highlighting, available on the VS Code Marketplace and GitHub. I work on this with Prof. Siddharth Srivastava and Dr. Rolf Jansen.

home.research.i-am-looking-for-co-rotati.text: I am looking for co-rotating and counter-rotating gas in the outer circumgalactic medium of L* galaxies, using sightline-based synthetic spectroscopy in TNG50-1. I have produced about 75,000 synthetic spectra in Lyα, C II λ1334 and Si III λ1206, and I am now classifying their kinematics and working through the uncertainties.

home.past-projects.i-studied-how-the-asy.text: I studied how the asymmetry of Fano resonance profiles changes with scattering angle, using a complex-valued w parameter that gives an angle-dependent Fano q. For the orbiting resonance in cold H–Kr elastic scattering, computed with the VPA phase-shift program, the asymmetry varies strongly with angle and is sensitive to the interatomic potential. I did this with Prof. Fumihiro Koike and Prof. Yoshiro Azuma, and published it as a first-author paper in the Indian Journal of Physics in 2026.
